items.title: The queue that moved
items.scenario: A hospital replaces paper requests with a portal. Request entry falls from six minutes to two, but patient transport still starts after forty minutes. Porters are shared across wards; dispatch prioritization is unchanged.
items.question: Which next framing best serves the stated goal of reducing time to transport?

choices.A: Standardize ward request forms and repeat the entry-time study to reduce front-end variation propagated into the transport queue.
choices.B: Improve portal adoption across wards before analyzing dispatch, because incomplete uptake may conceal the benefit of faster request entry.
choices.C: Add porter capacity during peak periods; the unchanged pickup delay indicates transport staffing should receive the first investment.
choices.D: Map request-to-pickup work and shared dispatch constraints, then identify which delays actually govern the transport outcome.

items.title: Solution in the initial need
items.scenario: A sponsor asks for a drone to inspect roof insulation. The underlying goal is to locate water ingress before winter; roof access is possible on some buildings and restricted on others. Budget and image interpretation capability are unresolved.
items.question: What is the most useful first concept decision?

choices.A: Set roof-coverage targets from the drone flight envelope, then evaluate image-interpretation tools against the resulting rate.
choices.B: Compare inspection means against ingress-detection needs, access conditions and interpretation capability before committing to a drone configuration.
choices.C: Validate drone inspection on accessible buildings and use that performance estimate to plan procurement for the restricted sites.
choices.D: Select an adaptable drone, then use a pilot inspection to determine which findings and reporting outcomes matter most.

items.title: Boundary versus ownership
items.scenario: A municipal flood-warning project defines its system-of-interest as the authority's own warning service, excluding supplier infrastructure. A commercial rainfall feed is required, and the authority remains accountable for warnings when that feed is delayed.
items.question: How should the supplier be represented?

choices.A: Allocate availability to the supplier contract and verify internal warning logic with timely inputs, assessing each organization separately.
choices.B: Include supplier infrastructure inside the implementation boundary and allocate its availability controls to the authority responsible for warnings.
choices.C: Model supplier delay as a fixed external parameter so internal design can proceed before delayed-feed response ownership is agreed.
choices.D: Keep the supplier external to the chosen boundary; specify its dependency contract and the authority's response to delayed data.

items.title: Conflicting outcomes
items.scenario: Airport operations wants shorter gate turnaround; maintenance wants enough inspection time; crews report increasing last-minute changes. The team proposes automation of the inspection signoff. No causal study is available.
items.question: Which proposed actions establish a defensible decision basis from the supplied facts, without first assuming a cause or a target?

choices.A: Define the competing turnaround, inspection and change-control outcomes, including the operating conditions in which each must be protected.
choices.B: Use maintenance ownership of signoff to assign it primary responsibility for delay, then measure the effect of automating its approval step.
choices.C: Adopt the fastest observed turnaround as the acceptance threshold for the new process, then investigate exceptions when that threshold is missed.
choices.D: Trace the timing of late changes, inspection work and decisions across roles to distinguish their contributions to the observed turnaround.

items.title: Extending a digital service
items.scenario: A rural telehealth service reduces appointment travel for patients with broadband. Patients without reliable connectivity miss more appointments after the clinic reduces its physical schedule. The project charter names access to care as the outcome.
items.question: Which revised system boundary best supports a design review?

choices.A: Review video uptime and completion rates, assigning physical-clinic access to another program with responsibility for those facilities.
choices.B: Review the complete appointment pathway, including connectivity support and physical alternatives, against the charter's access-to-care outcome.
choices.C: Define the service boundary around broadband users and report the remaining population separately to measure digital performance consistently.
choices.D: Model network availability for virtual appointments, keeping appointment scheduling outside the telecommunications review.

items.title: A cheaper pump cartridge
items.scenario: Cartridge A costs less and meets the specified flow range. It needs a calibration fixture available only at the factory. Cartridge B costs more but can be exchanged and checked in the field. Remote sites can tolerate at most a day without service.
items.question: What information most directly changes the purchase decision?

choices.A: Compare supplier calibration accreditation and reported accuracy uncertainty before deciding whether either cartridge offers sufficient measurement confidence.
choices.B: Compare purchase and factory-calibration costs across forecast volume, retaining the cheaper cartridge if its estimated lifecycle cost is lower.
choices.C: Compare supplier failure-rate estimates and select the longer-lived cartridge to minimize the expected frequency of restoration work.
choices.D: Estimate spare coverage, transport, repair turnaround and restoration at remote sites against the one-day service interruption limit.

items.title: Testing after handover

choices.C: Implement automatic diagnosis before handover, assigning the contractor the unresolved exceptions once the target diagnostic success rate is reached.

choices.B: Define who will provide compatible replacements and spares if the supplier ends support during the planned fifteen-year service period.
choices.C: Define how replacement modules receive and verify the authorized configuration before they are returned to the operating sensor network.

items.title: Reliability across a mission
items.scenario: Two alternatives have the same measured failure frequency during operation. One restores within minutes after a fault; the other requires a specialist visit. Missions are daily and unattended sites have limited access.
items.question: What conclusion follows?

choices.A: Compare failures over equal exposure and use the tighter uncertainty interval to choose between alternatives with similar observed reliability.
choices.B: Select the faster-restoring alternative and resolve purchase cost and specialist access during deployment planning.
choices.C: Compare restoration and access conditions alongside failure occurrence before estimating mission availability and lifecycle effort.
choices.D: Require field observations of both restoration processes before developing an availability estimate suitable for the purchase decision.

items.title: Transition is part of the system

choices.B: Qualify the final configuration and bridge legacy sites with temporary instructions during rollout.
choices.C: Include planned mixed configurations, transition responsibilities and recovery paths alongside the final all-new operational configuration.
choices.D: Accept each specified interface and confirm mixed-operation behavior during rollout, when actual legacy configurations become available.

items.title: Two channels, one supply
items.scenario: Two controllers execute different software and compare outputs. Both receive power from one converter, use the same clock and accept the same configuration file.
items.question: Which statement is best supported?

choices.A: Monitor the common supply and credit software diversity for the remaining faults once supply-failure detection is established.
choices.B: Software diversity addresses some causes; analyze shared supply, clock and configuration failures before claiming channel independence.
choices.C: Measure disagreement across representative inputs and use comparator coverage to establish independence between the channels.
choices.D: Combine separate software defect probabilities, then account for common hardware through the measured coverage of the comparator.

items.title: Correlated observations
items.scenario: A maintenance dashboard shows that faults are more frequent when technician overtime is high. Overtime also rises during severe weather and service disruptions.
items.question: Which investigation best discriminates explanations?

choices.A: Examine time ordering, weather exposure, fault-driven callouts and task workload to distinguish contributing, responding and common-cause explanations.
choices.B: Compare monthly overtime and faults across a longer observation period to reduce the influence of individual weather episodes.
choices.C: Limit overtime at the busiest sites and compare subsequent fault counts with the preceding quarter before investigating mechanisms.
choices.D: Compare technicians with different overtime at each site, holding assignment stable to separate workload effects from location.

items.title: A shared event in a tree
items.scenario: A fault tree is (A AND B) OR (A AND C). Event A represents the same loss of a shared supply wherever it appears.
items.question: Which minimal cut sets follow from that Boolean model?

choices.A: The minimal cut sets are {A,B} and {A,C}; either conjunction is sufficient, and both occurrences of A represent the same event.
choices.B: The minimal cut sets are {A1,B} and {A2,C}; repeated positions represent separate instances when evaluating the tree.
choices.C: The minimal cut sets are {A} and {B,C}; factoring the shared term separates its failure from the downstream conjunction.
choices.D: The minimal cut set is {A,B,C}; both branches appear beneath one top event and contribute to its combined condition.

items.title: A warning that causes more work
items.scenario: An alarm threshold is lowered. Detection rises, but operators receive many more alarms and begin delaying acknowledgment. Reported unresolved incidents also rise.
items.question: Which next model is most useful?

choices.A: Model how alarm load changes attention, acknowledgment and escalation, then connect those responses to unresolved events.
choices.B: Identify operators and shifts with the longest acknowledgment delays, prioritizing refresher training before changing detector or escalation settings.
choices.C: Refit the detector threshold against incident labels, increasing the penalty for missed events to offset the rise in unresolved cases.
choices.D: Apply the earlier acknowledgment distribution to the new alarm rate to estimate the additional staffing required.

items.title: Intermittent failure and a reset
items.scenario: Restarting a controller restores operation after a fault. The same fault returns under high load. Logs show buffer saturation before the restart but do not identify why data accumulates.
items.question: Which conclusion is justified?

choices.A: Investigate arrival, service and blocking mechanisms; buffer saturation is a causal lead, while reset recovery identifies a symptom.
choices.B: Reproduce reset recovery under increasing load and use repeated restoration to establish volatile-state corruption as the leading cause.
choices.C: Increase buffer capacity and close the investigation if the revised buffer prevents saturation throughout the high-load test.
choices.D: Compare peak utilization with published limits and replace the controller if it approaches capacity, postponing downstream service analysis.

items.title: A passing test on another revision
items.scenario: A latency report shows 180 ms on revision A against a 250 ms requirement. Revision B changes scheduling priorities and shares a processor with another service. No new timing observation is supplied.
items.question: What is the defensible disposition?

choices.A: Allocate the observed 70 ms margin to the new service and retest if predicted scheduling overhead exceeds that budget.
choices.B: Retain the report for unchanged algorithms and verify the added service separately, allocating scheduling effects to that component.
choices.C: Retain the revision-A result and reassess its applicability to B's scheduling and shared-resource conditions before claiming timing support.
choices.D: Record B as a timing failure pending a passing test, then replace the older report in the evidence index.

choices.B: The recorded configuration produced the observed tabletop-route and dummy-load behavior under the trial's stated conditions and measurement limits.
choices.C: The trial provides observations that can inform hypotheses, operating scenarios and procedures for a subsequent study in the intended ward context.

items.title: Zero observed failures

choices.B: Use reciprocal accumulated exposure as a conservative failure-rate estimate and carry that single rate into reliability planning.
choices.C: Exclude zero-event observations from reliability comparison and use the test to plan a campaign long enough to observe failures.
choices.D: Pool the twenty unit-hours into a survival duration and compare it directly with the uninterrupted mission required of one unit.

choices.B: Review the availability assumption and analyze outage/recovery behavior, preserving the existing proof as conditional evidence.
choices.C: Repeat the check with more requests to establish that the result scales with demand.
choices.D: Retain the proof and verify resource availability separately, treating successful recovery tests as support for the original continuous-availability assumption.

items.title: When an inspection is enough
items.scenario: A requirement specifies that an installation label show the serial number and supply rating. A neighboring requirement specifies alarm onset within 100 ms after a condition becomes true.

choices.A: Demonstrate label content and alarm onset together, having the reviewer confirm both during normal operation.
choices.B: Inspect label and timing configuration values, accepting both requirements when those stored values match the approved specification.
choices.C: Inspect label content and compare the nominal controller processing period with 100 ms to establish the alarm deadline.
choices.D: Inspect controlled label content; test alarm timing with defined stimulus, start/end events and observation resolution.

items.title: The timing reference
items.scenario: A need says an operator must be warned promptly when pressure becomes hazardous. The proposed requirement says the display refreshes every 100 ms. Sensor acquisition and hazard detection can take additional time.
items.question: What is the most important repair?

choices.A: Measure typical pressure-to-display delay and use its average to interpret prompt warning under normal operating conditions.
choices.B: Define the justified warning deadline between hazard and operator indication, then allocate acquisition, detection and presentation contributions against that end-to-end condition.
choices.C: Replace the display criterion with the sensor's maximum acquisition delay, because sensing the hazard is the first indispensable stage of the warning function.
choices.D: Retain display refresh and add sensor and detector deadlines, with each supplier defining the reference events for its contribution.

items.title: A measurable but misplaced requirement
items.scenario: A service robot requirement says its chassis shall be blue. A stakeholder need concerns staff finding the correct robot during a busy shift. No branding constraint or visibility study is supplied.
items.question: How should the requirement be reviewed?

choices.A: Replace the color criterion with a visibility threshold drawn from the robot's display specification, then verify that threshold using a controlled lighting test.
choices.B: Defer appearance decisions until staff trials are complete, so the requirements baseline contains only functions whose relation to the stakeholder need is already demonstrated.
choices.C: Trace blue to an identification need or binding constraint, then assess that proposed choice against staff behavior in the intended operating context.
choices.D: Keep blue as an inspectable design requirement and evaluate user identification separately, since objective component criteria and operational validation serve different purposes.

items.title: Decomposition loses a condition

items.question: What remains missing?

choices.A: Add measurable deadlines to each diagnostic so the two children fully specify the parent response to either sensing loss.
choices.B: The children require an allocation to separate sensors, because the parent's either-condition wording implies that sensing and shutdown must have redundant hardware paths.
choices.C: Both loss conditions are covered, but a common diagnostic identifier is needed to consolidate the children under the parent.
choices.D: The decomposition retains the two diagnostic triggers but omits the required shutdown response; define how either diagnosis causes the specified system action.

items.title: Resolving conflicting authorities

items.question: Which treatment preserves the decision basis?

choices.A: Use the newer meeting value for preliminary trades while retaining 40 kg in the contract register, then reconcile the two at the next baseline review.
choices.B: Trade options across the 40–45 kg range and recommend the highest-scoring design, treating the meeting note as evidence that the sponsor accepts that range.
choices.C: Use 40 kg as the obligation and 45 kg as a proposed change, showing the design consequence and the approval needed to adopt it.

items.title: Hazard versus a design prescription

choices.A: Retain the second processor as the derived safety requirement, then ask the supplier to define diagnostics and timing within the available hardware resources.
choices.B: Define the required control behavior, authority and conditions, then assess the second processor against those obligations and the actual failure dependencies.
choices.C: Convert the processor proposal into a redundancy requirement, then verify physical separation before developing the detection, command-arbitration and recovery behavior of the architecture.
choices.D: Allocate sensing to one processor and monitoring to another, then derive response requirements from the chosen monitoring mechanism.

items.title: A valid but stale command

items.title: Missing a decisive fact
items.scenario: A team asks whether an evacuation warning should trigger automatic door release. The building use, fire strategy, security constraints and failure modes of the release mechanism are unspecified.

choices.C: Propose manual release as the default because it preserves human authority, then measure whether the expected operator response meets the evacuation timing needs.
choices.D: Request the complete building design and fire documentation before comparing release options, so no preliminary recommendation relies on a provisional interpretation of intended use.

items.title: An estimate becomes a fact
items.scenario: A preliminary model assumes a 20-minute restoration time because no maintenance data exists. Several slides later, the executive summary calls this the measured restoration time.
items.question: What correction is needed?

choices.B: Restore the value's assumption status and identify which conclusions depend on it, preserving useful calculations as explicitly conditional results.
choices.C: Exclude the model's results from the decision package until restoration data is obtained, because an assumed input cannot support any useful engineering comparison.
choices.D: Substitute a longer restoration allowance and retain the conclusion, using conservatism to cover the missing measurements.

items.title: US Airways 1549: decision time in a simulation
items.scenario: The NTSB's report on the 2009 US Airways 1549 accident distinguishes immediate-return simulator attempts from scenarios including crew decision time. An immediate turn toward an airport does not represent the same starting conditions as the actual crew's situation.
items.question: What is the strongest transferable lesson?

choices.B: Compare alternatives using the information and recognition-to-action timing available at the actual decision point, stating what each simulation assumes.
choices.C: Compare aircraft capability from the instant of hazard onset, then treat recognition and diagnosis as separate training factors outside the alternative-feasibility assessment.
choices.D: Use the delayed simulator attempt as the representative case, then extrapolate its outcome to the range of feasible return decisions in the actual event.

items.title: A borderline result
items.scenario: A dimension has an upper acceptance limit of 10.00 mm. A measurement reads 9.99 mm, with stated expanded uncertainty of 0.03 mm. The project has not defined an acceptance decision rule.

choices.C: Accept the item using the measured value because the requirement specifies a limit on dimension, while instrument uncertainty belongs in the laboratory quality record.
choices.D: Report the result and uncertainty, then resolve or apply the agreed acceptance decision rule before assigning the item a disposition.

items.title: The handover with no receiver

choices.C: Send exceptions to both shift supervisors and add a dashboard of unread messages, retaining the current shared responsibility arrangement.

items.title: Explaining verification and validation
items.scenario: A junior engineer asks why a product can pass every specified test and still fail its users. The team has measured compliance with its written requirements but has not observed the intended users in the operating context.

choices.B: Passing requirements supports intended use when stakeholder approval is recorded; observation is mainly needed to discover improvements for the next release.
choices.C: Verification checks implementation details and validation repeats the tests at system level; the missing user observation should therefore repeat system requirements.
choices.D: The specification may omit intended-use needs: supplement its tests with interviews, treating stakeholder agreement as sufficient validation of the implemented product.
